title: Fractions — First Steps
blurb: Fractions as parts of a whole, equivalent fractions, comparing, improper fractions and mixed numbers, and adding and subtracting with like denominators.

lessons.title: What a Fraction Is
lessons.concreteComparison: A round bread is cut into $8$ EQUAL pieces and you eat $3$. The amount you ate has a name: $\frac{3}{8}$ of the bread. The bottom number says what size the pieces are (eighths — eight of them make the whole); the top number counts how many you took. Two numbers, one amount — and the word EQUAL is doing all the honest work.
lessons.objective: Read and write fractions as equal parts of a whole, find a fraction of a set, place fractions on the number line, and recognise when parts are NOT equal.
concept: **The denominator names the piece.** The bottom number says how many EQUAL parts make one whole — eighths mean eight equal parts. The top number, the numerator, counts how many of those parts you have: $\frac{3}{8}$ is three pieces of the eight-piece size.

**Unit fractions are the atoms.** $\frac{1}{8}$ is ONE piece; every fraction is a stack of unit fractions — $\frac{3}{8}$ is $\frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{8}$. And eight eighths rebuild the whole: $\frac{8}{8} = 1$.

**Fractions live on the number line and in sets.** $\frac{3}{4}$ is a POINT between $0$ and $1$ (split the unit into four, count three); and $\frac{3}{4}$ OF $12$ apples is $9$ apples — split the set into four equal groups of $3$, take three groups.
lessons.keyIdea: The denominator says what size the equal pieces are; the numerator counts them. Same two numbers work for shapes, sets, and points on the number line.

facts.title: Numerator over denominator
facts.explanation: Bottom names the piece size; top counts the pieces.

facts.title: The whole rebuilt
facts.explanation: All the pieces together are exactly one whole — the denominator's promise.

workedExamples.statement: A bread is cut into $8$ equal pieces; you eat $3$ and your brother eats $5$. What fraction did each eat, and what do the two fractions make together?
workedExamples.note: Count pieces; the whole is eight eighths.
workedExamples.solution: You: $\frac{3}{8}$. Brother: $\frac{5}{8}$. Together: $\frac{3}{8} + \frac{5}{8} = \frac{8}{8} = 1$ — the whole bread, as it must be.

workedExamples.note: Split into four equal groups, take three.
workedExamples.solution: Four equal groups of $12 \div 4 = 3$ apples each; take three groups: $3 \times 3 = 9$ apples. So $\frac{3}{4}$ of $12$ is $9$.

commonMistakes.text: Counting unequal parts as a fraction — calling a lopsided 3-of-5 cut "3/5".
commonMistakes.correction: Fractions require EQUAL parts. If the pieces differ, the denominator's name is a lie — cut again or count differently.

commonMistakes.text: Reading 3/8 as "3 and 8" — two separate numbers.
commonMistakes.correction: A fraction is ONE amount: three pieces of the eighth size. The bar is not a comma.

tryIt.statement: A week has $7$ days; you train on $4$ of them. What fraction of the week do you train, and what fraction is training-free?
tryIt.solution: Training: $\frac{4}{7}$. Free: $\frac{3}{7}$. Together $\frac{4}{7} + \frac{3}{7} = \frac{7}{7} = 1$ — the whole week.
Five equal groups of $4$; take two: $\frac{2}{5}$ of $20 = 8$.

steps.title: Bottom names, top counts
beats: Cut a whole into EQUAL parts: the denominator (bottom) says how many parts make the whole — that's the piece's NAME. Eighths: eight per whole.
The numerator (top) counts how many pieces you have: $\frac{3}{8}$ is three pieces of the eighth size.
Every fraction is a stack of unit fractions — $\frac{3}{8} = \frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{8}$ — and all the pieces together rebuild the whole: $\frac{8}{8} = 1$.

steps.title: Reading fractions
steps.intro: Name the piece, count the pieces.

examples.prompt: A bread in $8$ equal pieces: you eat $3$, your brother $5$. Fractions?
What fraction of an hour is $45$ minutes?
steps: An hour is $60$ minutes; each minute is $\frac{1}{60}$ of it.
$45$ minutes is $\frac{45}{60}$ — which you'll soon write as $\frac{3}{4}$.

steps.title: Count the pieces
steps.intro: Equal parts only — check before counting.

problems.prompt: A pizza is cut into $6$ equal slices and $5$ are taken. The fraction taken is:
problems.explanation: Six equal slices make the whole (sixths); five are taken: $\frac{5}{6}$. And $\frac{1}{6}$ remains: $\frac{5}{6} + \frac{1}{6} = 1$.

problems.prompt: You train $4$ days of a $7$-day week. The training-free fraction is:
problems.explanation: $7 - 4 = 3$ free days of the seven: $\frac{3}{7}$.

problems.prompt: How many $\frac{1}{5}$ pieces make one whole?
problems.explanation: The denominator's promise: five fifths rebuild the whole — $\frac{5}{5} = 1$.

steps.title: The equal-parts rule
steps.prompt: A circle is cut into $4$ parts of DIFFERENT sizes, and one part is shaded. Is the shaded amount $\frac{1}{4}$?
options: yes — one of four parts is always a quarter
yes, if the shaded part is the biggest
steps.explanation: The denominator names a piece SIZE, and that only means something when all pieces share it. One unequal part of four could be almost anything — the word "quarter" would lie. (With equal parts, $4 \times \frac{1}{4} = 1$.)

steps.title: Fractions are older than the alphabet
steps.body: Egyptian scribes four thousand years ago wrote almost everything using UNIT fractions — amounts like $\frac{2}{5}$ had to be expressed as sums such as $\frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{15}$. Check it: that sum really is $\frac{2}{5}$. Your notation is friendlier — but the unit-fraction atoms are the same ones.

steps.title: Sets and the number line
beats: Fractions measure SETS too: $\frac{3}{4}$ of $12$ apples — split the set into $4$ equal groups ($3$ each), take $3$ groups: $9$ apples.
And fractions are POINTS: on the number line, $\frac{3}{4}$ lives between $0$ and $1$ — split the unit into four, count three marks.
One notation, three pictures — shape, set, point. The denominator names the split in all three.

steps.title: Fractions of sets
steps.intro: Split into denominator-many groups; take numerator-many.

steps: Three equal groups of $6$; take two.

steps.title: Of a set, on a line
steps.intro: Groups for sets; marks for lines.

problems.explanation: Five groups of $4$; take two: $8$.
Eight groups of $3$; take three: $9$.

problems.prompt: On a number line from $0$ to $1$ split into sixths, the point $\frac{5}{6}$ sits:
problems.explanation: Five of the six marks along: one short of the whole — $\frac{5}{6} + \frac{1}{6} = 1$.

steps.title: Which picture?
steps.prompt: $\frac{3}{4}$ of $12$ students wear deel. How many students is that?
steps.explanation: Split $12$ into four equal groups of $3$; three groups wear deel: $9$ students.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Denominator names the piece size (equal parts per whole); numerator counts pieces.
Unit fractions are the atoms; all the pieces together make exactly 1.
Fractions of a set: split into denominator-many groups, take numerator-many.
On the number line a fraction is a point — split the unit, count the marks.
No equal parts, no fraction — the equal-parts rule is the foundation.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: Mixed pictures below — shapes, sets, and number lines. Say the piece's NAME (sixths, eighths...) before answering each.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: All three pictures of a fraction.

problems.prompt: A chocolate bar of $10$ equal squares: you eat $7$. Fraction remaining:
problems.explanation: $10 - 7 = 3$ squares of the tenth size remain: $\frac{3}{10}$.
Six groups of $5$; take four: $20$.

problems.prompt: How many $\frac{1}{12}$ pieces make one whole?
problems.explanation: Twelve twelfths: $\frac{12}{12} = 1$.

problems.prompt: What fraction of a metre is $30$ cm?
problems.explanation: A metre is $100$ cm; each cm is $\frac{1}{100}$ of it: $\frac{30}{100}$ (soon you'll also call it $\frac{3}{10}$).

problems.prompt: A garden is split into $8$ equal beds, $8$ flowers in each. Roses fill $\frac{5}{8}$ of the garden. How many flowers are roses?
problems.explanation: Five of the eight beds are roses: $5 \times 8 = 40$ flowers — which is exactly $\frac{5}{8}$ of the garden's $64$.

steps.title: You've finished "What a Fraction Is"
steps.body: One notation, three pictures — and the equal-parts rule underneath them all. Next: the surprising fact that one amount wears MANY fraction names, and how to switch between them.

lessons.title: Equivalent Fractions
lessons.concreteComparison: Half a bread is half a bread — whether you cut that half into $2$ quarters, $3$ sixths, or $4$ eighths. $\frac{1}{2}$, $\frac{2}{4}$, $\frac{3}{6}$, $\frac{4}{8}$: four names, one amount. Splitting every piece into smaller ones changes the NUMBERS but not the bread — and that's the whole secret of equivalent fractions.
lessons.objective: Make equivalent fractions by multiplying or dividing the numerator and denominator by the same number, and reduce a fraction to simplest form.
concept: **Split every piece the same way.** Cut each half into $3$: the $1$ half becomes $3$ pieces, the $2$-per-whole becomes $6$-per-whole — $\frac{1}{2} = \frac{3}{6}$. Numerator and denominator both got multiplied by $3$, and the amount never moved.

**Merging runs it backwards.** If numerator and denominator share a factor, glue that many small pieces into one big one: $\frac{9}{12}$ — divide both by $3$ — is $\frac{3}{4}$. Same amount, chunkier pieces.

**Simplest form** is the fully-merged name: numerator and denominator share no factor but $1$. Every fraction has exactly one simplest name — $\frac{9}{12}$, $\frac{6}{8}$, $\frac{75}{100}$ all answer to $\frac{3}{4}$.
lessons.keyIdea: Multiply or divide top AND bottom by the same number and the amount doesn't move — only its name changes. The simplest name is the one with nothing left to divide.

facts.title: The splitting move
facts.explanation: Same amount, finer pieces — top and bottom scale together.

facts.title: The merging move
facts.explanation: Divide out the shared factor; the fully-merged name is simplest form.

workedExamples.note: What multiplied the 3 into 12? The top gets the same.
workedExamples.solution: $3 \times 4 = 12$, so the numerator scales by $4$ too: $2 \times 4 = 8$. $\frac{2}{3} = \frac{8}{12}$.
$18$ and $24$ share the factor $6$: divide both — $\frac{18 \div 6}{24 \div 6} = \frac{3}{4}$. Nothing but $1$ divides both $3$ and $4$, so $\frac{3}{4}$ is the simplest name.

commonMistakes.text: Adding the same number to top and bottom — 1/2 = 2/3 "because I added 1 to both".
commonMistakes.correction: Equivalence comes from MULTIPLYING or dividing both, never adding. Adding 1 to both moves the amount: 1/2 ≠ 2/3 (a half is less than two-thirds).

commonMistakes.text: Stopping the simplification early — calling 12/16 "simplified" as 6/8.
commonMistakes.correction: 6 and 8 still share a 2: keep dividing until the only shared factor is 1. 12/16 = 6/8 = 3/4 — simplest form is the END of the road.

tryIt.solution: Divide both by $15$: $\frac{3}{4}$. (Or by $5$ then $3$ — the road doesn't matter, the end does.)

steps.title: Split the pieces, keep the amount
beats: Cut every piece of $\frac{1}{2}$ into three: now there are $3$ pieces of the $6$-per-whole size — $\frac{1}{2} = \frac{3}{6}$. The bread never moved.
The rule underneath: multiply numerator AND denominator by the same number. $\frac{1 \times 3}{2 \times 3} = \frac{3}{6}$.
It must be the SAME number top and bottom — that's what keeps the splitting honest.

steps.title: Scaling up
steps.intro: Find what scaled the denominator; scale the numerator to match.

steps.title: Scale to match
steps.intro: Same multiplier, top and bottom.

problems.explanation: $5 \to 20$ is $\times 4$: top becomes $12$.
$5 \to 35$ is $\times 7$: bottom becomes $42$.

problems.prompt: Which fraction is NOT equal to $\frac{1}{2}$?
problems.explanation: $\frac{6}{12}$ and $\frac{50}{100}$ both merge back to $\frac{1}{2}$; $\frac{5}{12}$ falls short of it.

steps.title: The forbidden move
steps.prompt: A student writes $\frac{1}{2} = \frac{2}{3}$ "because I added $1$ to the top and bottom". This is:
steps.explanation: Adding moves the amount: $\frac{1}{2}$ is genuinely less than $\frac{2}{3}$. Only MULTIPLYING (or dividing) both keeps the bread in place.

steps.title: Why 75/100 shows up everywhere
steps.body: Percent is just an equivalent-fraction convention: every amount renamed with denominator $100$. "$75\%$" IS $\frac{75}{100}$, which is $\frac{3}{4}$ in simplest form. When you meet percents next year, you already know the whole trick.

steps.title: Merging, and the simplest name
beats: Run the splitting backwards: if top and bottom share a factor, DIVIDE it out — merge small pieces into big ones. $\frac{9}{12} \to \frac{3}{4}$ (divide by $3$).
Keep merging until nothing but $1$ divides both — that's SIMPLEST FORM, the fraction's shortest name.
Any road works: $\frac{12}{16} \to \frac{6}{8} \to \frac{3}{4}$, or straight there dividing by $4$. The end is the same because the simplest name is unique.

steps.title: Down to simplest form
steps.intro: Divide out shared factors until none remain.

steps: (Or by $15$ in one hop — same destination.)

steps.title: Simplest form
steps.intro: Merge until only 1 divides both.

problems.explanation: Divide both by $4$: $\frac{4}{5}$. ($\frac{8}{10}$ merges only halfway.)
Divide both by $5$: $\frac{7}{10}$ — and $7, 10$ share nothing more.

problems.prompt: Which is already in simplest form?
problems.explanation: $8$ and $15$ share only $1$. The others still merge: $\frac{9}{12} = \frac{3}{4}$, $\frac{10}{25} = \frac{2}{5}$.

steps.title: Halfway is not done
steps.prompt: A student simplifies $\frac{12}{16}$ to $\frac{6}{8}$ and stops. The finished answer is:
options: $\frac{12}{16}$ — it was fine as it was
steps.explanation: Simplest form is the END of the merging road: $\frac{6}{8}$ still divides by $2$ to $\frac{3}{4}$, and there the road ends.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Multiply top AND bottom by the same number: finer pieces, same amount.
Divide out shared factors: chunkier pieces, same amount.
Adding to top and bottom moves the amount — the forbidden move.
Simplest form = nothing but 1 divides both; every fraction has exactly one.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: For each item, say which move you're using — splitting (×) or merging (÷) — before touching the numbers.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Both moves, in both directions.

problems.explanation: $9 \to 36$ is $\times 4$: top becomes $16$.
Divide both by $12$: $\frac{2}{3}$. The other options merge only partway.

problems.prompt: $\frac{45}{60}$ of an hour is the same as:
problems.explanation: $\frac{45}{60}$ merges by $15$ to $\frac{3}{4}$ — the $45$-minute mark.

problems.prompt: Which pair are two names for one amount?
problems.explanation: Both merge to $\frac{3}{5}$: $\frac{6}{10} = \frac{9}{15} = \frac{3}{5}$.
All the pieces together: one whole — however fine the cut.

steps.title: You've finished "Equivalent Fractions"
steps.body: Splitting and merging — the two moves that let one amount wear many names — power everything ahead: comparing fractions and (next year) adding ones with different denominators. Next: which of two fractions is bigger?

lessons.title: Comparing Fractions
lessons.concreteComparison: Who ate more bread: you with $\frac{3}{5}$ of yours, or your friend with $\frac{3}{8}$ of hers? Same COUNT of pieces — three — but your pieces are fifths and hers are eighths, and fifths are bigger (fewer pieces make the whole). Three big pieces beat three small ones. Comparing fractions is always about piece size versus piece count.
lessons.objective: Compare fractions with the same denominator, the same numerator, and using the benchmarks one-half and one — choosing the fastest strategy each time.
concept: **Same denominator: count wins.** Pieces are the same size, so more pieces is more: $\frac{5}{8} > \frac{3}{8}$.
**Same numerator: piece size wins — backwards.** A bigger denominator means MORE pieces per whole, so each is SMALLER: $\frac{3}{5} > \frac{3}{8}$, because fifths beat eighths.

**Different everything: use a benchmark.** Is each fraction more or less than $\frac{1}{2}$? $\frac{4}{9}$ is under half ($4$ is less than half of $9$), $\frac{5}{8}$ is over half ($5$ is more than half of $8$): so $\frac{4}{9} < \frac{5}{8}$ without any common name.
lessons.keyIdea: Same-size pieces: count them. Same count: bigger denominator means smaller pieces. Neither: park each fraction against one-half or one, and compare the parks.

facts.title: Same numerator flips
facts.explanation: More pieces per whole = smaller pieces — the denominator compares backwards.

facts.title: The half benchmark
facts.explanation: Double the numerator against the denominator: 8 < 9 (under half); 10 > 8 (over half).

workedExamples.note: Same count — so compare the piece sizes.
workedExamples.solution: Both are three pieces, but fifths are bigger than eighths ($5$ pieces per whole against $8$). Three big beats three small: $\frac{3}{5} > \frac{3}{8}$.

workedExamples.statement: Compare $\frac{4}{9}$ and $\frac{5}{8}$ using the half benchmark.
workedExamples.note: Neither denominators nor numerators match — park each against 1/2.
workedExamples.solution: $\frac{4}{9}$: half of $9$ is $4\frac{1}{2}$, and $4$ falls short — under half. $\frac{5}{8}$: half of $8$ is $4$, and $5$ exceeds it — over half. Under beats over... the other way: $\frac{4}{9} < \frac{1}{2} < \frac{5}{8}$.

commonMistakes.text: Bigger denominator = bigger fraction — reading 3/8 > 3/5 because 8 > 5.
commonMistakes.correction: The denominator counts pieces PER WHOLE: more pieces means each is smaller. With equal numerators the bigger denominator LOSES.
Five small pieces can be less than four big ones: 5/9 is barely over half while 4/5 is nearly whole. Match the pieces (or benchmark) before counting.

tryIt.solution: Benchmark: $\frac{7}{12}$ is over half ($14 > 12$), $\frac{5}{11}$ is under half ($10 < 11$): $\frac{7}{12} > \frac{5}{11}$.

steps.title: Count, or size — never both blindly
beats: Same DENOMINATOR: the pieces match, so the count decides — $\frac{5}{8} > \frac{3}{8}$.
Same NUMERATOR: the counts match, so piece size decides — and it compares BACKWARDS: $\frac{3}{5} > \frac{3}{8}$, because a whole cut into five gives bigger pieces than one cut into eight.
The backwards rule surprises everyone once: more pieces per whole = smaller pieces. Say it until it stops surprising.

steps.title: Matching pieces or matching counts
steps.intro: Spot which part matches; the other part decides.

steps: Same count (three), different sizes: fifths beat eighths.

steps.title: Match and compare
steps.intro: Which part matches? The other decides.

problems.explanation: Same sevenths — more of them wins: $\frac{6}{7}$.
Same count, different sizes: thirds are three-per-whole, ninths nine-per-whole — thirds are bigger.
Five pieces each — the finest cut (twelfths) gives the smallest pieces: $\frac{5}{12}$.

steps.title: The backwards rule
steps.explanation: One piece each, but a whole cut into ten gives far smaller pieces than one cut into four. The denominator compares backwards.

steps.title: The quarter-pound lesson
steps.body: A famous marketing failure: a chain sold third-pound burgers against quarter-pounders at the same price — and customers refused, reasoning that $3 < 4$ meant less meat. The backwards rule in the wild: $\frac{1}{3}$ of a pound is MORE than $\frac{1}{4}$.

steps.title: Benchmarks — park against a half
beats: Different numerators AND denominators? Park each fraction against $\frac{1}{2}$: double the numerator and compare with the denominator. $\frac{4}{9}$: $8 < 9$ — under half. $\frac{5}{8}$: $10 > 8$ — over half.
Under beats over is settled instantly: $\frac{4}{9} < \frac{5}{8}$, no common name needed.
The other great benchmark is $1$: $\frac{7}{8}$ misses one whole by a thin $\frac{1}{8}$, while $\frac{5}{4}$ has already passed it.

steps.title: Benchmark comparisons
steps.intro: Double the top; compare with the bottom.

steps.title: Park and decide
steps.intro: Half and one — the two great landmarks.

problems.explanation: Double the top: $6$, against the bottom $7$ — falls short: under half.
Their gaps to $1$: $\frac{1}{8}, \frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{6}$ — and eighths are the smallest gap (backwards rule again).

steps.title: Numerals lie across sizes
steps.prompt: $\frac{5}{9}$ or $\frac{4}{5}$ — a student picks $\frac{5}{9}$ "because $5 > 4$". The truth:
options: $\frac{4}{5} > \frac{5}{9}$ — four big pieces beat five small ones
steps.explanation: $\frac{4}{5}$ is one small fifth short of a whole; $\frac{5}{9}$ barely clears half. Counting numerators across different piece sizes is the classic trap.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Same denominator: more pieces wins.
Same numerator: bigger denominator = smaller pieces — the backwards rule.
Benchmarks: double the top against the bottom for the half test; measure gaps to 1.
Never compare bare numerators across different piece sizes.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: Name your strategy before each answer — same-pieces, same-count, or benchmark. The naming is faster than any computation.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Pick the fastest road each time.

problems.explanation: Same tenths: $7 < 9$.
Same count — fifths beat elevenths: $>$.
Half test: $12 > 11$ (over) against $8 < 9$ (under).
$\frac{3}{8}$ is under half ($6 < 8$), $\frac{3}{4}$ is over ($6 > 4$).

problems.prompt: Two runners finish $\frac{5}{6}$ and $\frac{7}{9}$ of the same trail. Who ran further?
problems.explanation: Gaps to the finish: $\frac{1}{6}$ against $\frac{2}{9}$ — and $\frac{1}{6} = \frac{3}{18}$ is less than $\frac{2}{9} = \frac{4}{18}$: the first is closer to done.

steps.title: You've finished "Comparing Fractions"
steps.body: Count against size, and two great landmarks — that's the whole comparing toolkit. Next: fractions that outgrow the whole, and the two names they answer to.

lessons.title: Improper Fractions & Mixed Numbers
lessons.concreteComparison: Seven guests each take a third of a bread. You need seven thirds — $\frac{7}{3}$ — which is more than two whole breads and a piece besides. The SAME amount has two honest names: $\frac{7}{3}$ (count the pieces) and $2\frac{1}{3}$ (count the wholes, then the leftover). Switching between the names is division you already know.
lessons.objective: Read improper fractions and mixed numbers as two names for one amount, and convert both ways using division with remainders.
concept: **Top-heavy fractions pass the whole.** When the numerator reaches the denominator you have exactly $1$; beyond it you're past a whole — $\frac{7}{3}$ is more than $2$ but less than $3$. These are IMPROPER fractions (nothing wrong with them — just top-heavy).
**Improper → mixed is division.** $\frac{7}{3}$: divide — $7 \div 3 = 2$ r $1$. Two wholes, one third left: $2\frac{1}{3}$. The remainder keeps its denominator.

**Mixed → improper multiplies back.** $3\frac{2}{5}$: each whole is $\frac{5}{5}$, so three wholes are $\frac{15}{5}$, plus the $\frac{2}{5}$: $\frac{17}{5}$ — the division receipt $3 \times 5 + 2 = 17$ in fraction clothes.
lessons.keyIdea: Improper fractions and mixed numbers are two names for one amount, and division with remainders converts between them: quotient = wholes, remainder = the leftover pieces.

facts.title: Improper to mixed
facts.explanation: Quotient counts the wholes; the remainder keeps its denominator.

facts.title: Mixed to improper
facts.explanation: Wholes times pieces-per-whole, plus the loose pieces — the receipt, refolded.

workedExamples.note: Divide; the remainder keeps the denominator.
workedExamples.solution: $23 \div 6 = 3$ r $5$: three wholes and five sixths — $3\frac{5}{6}$. Receipt: $3 \times 6 + 5 = 23$ ✓.
Four wholes are $4 \times 8 = 32$ eighths; add the three loose ones: $\frac{35}{8}$.

commonMistakes.text: Dropping the remainder's denominator — writing 23/6 as "3 r 5" or "3.5".
commonMistakes.correction: The leftover is five SIXTHS: 3 5/6. The remainder is a fraction with the same denominator, not a decimal and not a bare number.

commonMistakes.text: Adding wholes to the numerator without scaling — 4 3/8 = 7/8.
commonMistakes.correction: A whole is EIGHT eighths, not one. Four wholes contribute 32 eighths: 4 3/8 = 35/8.

tryIt.solution: Two wholes are $18$ ninths; plus five: $\frac{23}{9}$.

steps.title: Past the whole
beats: When the numerator reaches the denominator, you hold exactly one whole: $\frac{3}{3} = 1$. Past it, the fraction is TOP-HEAVY — improper: $\frac{7}{3}$ is more than $2$, less than $3$.
Its second name counts wholes first: $\frac{7}{3} = 2\frac{1}{3}$ — two wholes and a third.
The converter is division with remainders, which you own: $7 \div 3 = 2$ r $1$ — quotient counts wholes, the remainder keeps its denominator.

steps.title: Improper to mixed
steps.intro: Divide; wholes from the quotient, pieces from the remainder.

steps.title: Count the wholes
steps.intro: Divide, then dress the remainder.

problems.explanation: $11 \div 4 = 2$ r $3$: two wholes and three quarters.
$20 \div 5 = 4$ with nothing left: four exact wholes.

steps.title: Where does it live?
steps.prompt: On the number line, $\frac{7}{3}$ sits between:
steps.explanation: $\frac{6}{3} = 2$ and $\frac{9}{3} = 3$ — seven thirds lands a third past $2$.

steps.title: "Improper" is a terrible name
steps.body: There is nothing wrong with a top-heavy fraction — mathematicians prefer them, because they add and multiply more cleanly than mixed numbers. The name is a fossil from centuries-old textbooks. Use whichever name serves the moment: mixed to SAY an amount, improper to COMPUTE with it.

steps.title: Mixed to improper — the receipt refolded
beats: To turn $3\frac{2}{5}$ improper, turn the wholes into fifths first: each whole is $\frac{5}{5}$, so three wholes are $\frac{15}{5}$.
Add the loose pieces: $\frac{15}{5} + \frac{2}{5} = \frac{17}{5}$. In one line: wholes × denominator + numerator, over the same denominator.
That formula IS the division receipt ($3 \times 5 + 2 = 17$) — the two conversions are one fact, read in both directions.

steps.title: Refolding the receipt
steps.intro: Wholes × pieces-per-whole + loose pieces.

steps.title: Make it top-heavy
steps.intro: Scale the wholes; add the loose pieces.

problems.explanation: $2\frac{3}{4} = \frac{11}{4}$, and $\frac{12}{4} = 3$: twelve quarters beat eleven.

steps.title: The seven-eighths trap
steps.prompt: A student converts $4\frac{3}{8}$ to $\frac{7}{8}$ by adding $4 + 3$. The slip:
options: a whole is EIGHT eighths — four wholes contribute $32$, not $4$
steps.explanation: Wholes must be renamed into the piece size first: $4 \times 8 = 32$ eighths, plus $3$ gives $\frac{35}{8}$ — an amount past four, while $\frac{7}{8}$ is less than one.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Numerator reaches the denominator: exactly one whole; beyond: top-heavy (improper).
Improper → mixed: divide; quotient = wholes, remainder keeps its denominator.
Mixed → improper: wholes × denominator + numerator, same denominator.
Both conversions are one division receipt, read in two directions.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: Convert each one BOTH ways — there and back — and check you return to where you started. Round trips catch every slip.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Two names, full round trips.

problems.explanation: $17 \div 5 = 3$ r $2$: $3\frac{2}{5}$. ($2\frac{7}{5}$ smuggles a whole inside the fraction.)

problems.prompt: Between which whole numbers does $\frac{29}{6}$ sit?
problems.explanation: $\frac{24}{6} = 4$ and $\frac{30}{6} = 5$: it lands at $4\frac{5}{6}$.

problems.prompt: A recipe needs $\frac{9}{4}$ cups of flour. In whole cups and quarters that is:
problems.explanation: $9 \div 4 = 2$ r $1$: two full cups and one quarter-cup.

problems.prompt: Which pair are the SAME amount?

steps.title: You've finished "Improper Fractions & Mixed Numbers"
steps.body: Division with remainders turned out to be fraction notation in disguise — the remainder was a numerator all along. Last stop: adding and subtracting fractions whose pieces already match.

lessons.title: Adding & Subtracting Fractions
lessons.concreteComparison: You eat $\frac{3}{8}$ of a bread; your sister eats $\frac{2}{8}$. Together: five pieces of the eighth size — $\frac{5}{8}$. NOT $\frac{5}{16}$: nobody recut the bread. When the pieces already match, adding fractions is just counting pieces — the denominator is the pieces' name, and names don't add.
lessons.objective: Add and subtract fractions with like denominators, simplify results, handle sums past one whole, and subtract a fraction from a whole number.
concept: **Count the pieces; keep the name.** $\frac{3}{8} + \frac{2}{8} = \frac{5}{8}$: three eighths plus two eighths is five eighths — exactly like $3$ sheep $+ 2$ sheep $= 5$ sheep. Adding the denominators would rename the pieces mid-count: the one unforgivable move.
**Results like to be simplified.** $\frac{3}{8} + \frac{1}{8} = \frac{4}{8}$ — which answers to its simplest name, $\frac{1}{2}$. Finish every sum with a merge check.

**Past one whole, and back from one.** $\frac{5}{6} + \frac{4}{6} = \frac{9}{6} = 1\frac{1}{2}$ — top-heavy sums convert to mixed. And to subtract FROM a whole, rename it first: $1 = \frac{4}{4}$, so $1 - \frac{3}{4} = \frac{1}{4}$.
lessons.keyIdea: Like pieces add and subtract by their counts — the denominator is a name, not a number to add. Simplify the result, convert top-heavy answers, and rename wholes before subtracting from them.

facts.title: Count, don't rename
facts.explanation: Pieces of one size add like objects of one kind; the name stays.

facts.title: Wholes rename before subtracting
facts.explanation: Dress the whole in the needed denominator, then count.

workedExamples.statement: Add $\frac{3}{8} + \frac{2}{8}$, and explain why the answer is not $\frac{5}{16}$.
workedExamples.note: The pieces already match — just count.
workedExamples.solution: Three eighths plus two eighths is five eighths: $\frac{5}{8}$. Writing $\frac{5}{16}$ would claim the pieces became sixteenths — but nobody recut the bread. (And $\frac{5}{16}$ is LESS than $\frac{3}{8}$ alone — an addition that shrinks is its own alarm bell.)
$\frac{5}{6} + \frac{4}{6} = \frac{9}{6}$ — top-heavy. Convert: $9 \div 6 = 1$ r $3$, so $1\frac{3}{6}$, and $\frac{3}{6}$ simplifies: $1\frac{1}{2}$.

commonMistakes.correction: The denominator NAMES the pieces; it doesn't count anything. Five eighths, same name: 5/8. If your "sum" is smaller than one addend, this is what happened.

commonMistakes.text: Refusing to subtract from a whole number — "1 − 3/4 can't be done, 1 has no fourths".
commonMistakes.correction: It does once you rename it: 1 = 4/4. Then 4/4 − 3/4 = 1/4. Wholes wear any denominator you need.

steps.title: Count the pieces, keep the name
beats: When denominators match, the pieces are the same size — so adding is COUNTING: $\frac{3}{8} + \frac{2}{8} = \frac{5}{8}$, exactly like $3$ sheep $+ 2$ sheep.
The denominator is the pieces' NAME. Adding names ($\frac{5}{16}$) claims someone recut the bread — and produces a "sum" smaller than one of the addends. An addition that shrinks is an alarm bell.
Subtraction counts the other way: $\frac{7}{10} - \frac{3}{10} = \frac{4}{10}$ — then simplify: $\frac{2}{5}$.

steps.title: Matching pieces
steps.intro: Add or subtract the counts; the name rides along.

steps: Count: $3 + 2 = 5$ pieces of the eighth size.
$\frac{5}{8}$ — and note $\frac{5}{16}$ would be SMALLER than $\frac{3}{8}$: the alarm bell.

steps.title: Same-name arithmetic
steps.intro: Counts move; names don't.

problems.explanation: Six ninths — which merges to $\frac{2}{3}$. ($\frac{6}{18}$ added the names.)
$\frac{6}{12}$, which is $\frac{1}{2}$ in simplest form.
$2 + 3 + 1 = 6$ sevenths: $\frac{6}{7}$ — one seventh short of the whole.

steps.title: The alarm bell
steps.prompt: A student computes $\frac{1}{4} + \frac{2}{4} = \frac{3}{8}$. What gives the error away instantly?
options: $\frac{3}{8}$ is SMALLER than the addend $\frac{2}{4}$ — adding can't shrink
steps.explanation: Adding positive amounts must grow: but $\frac{3}{8} < \frac{2}{4} = \frac{4}{8}$. The denominators were added — the pieces are still quarters: $\frac{3}{4}$.

steps.title: Same rule, every size
steps.body: "Three eighths plus two eighths is five eighths" works for exactly the same reason as "three metres plus two metres is five metres" — you can only count things that share a unit. Next year, adding $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3}$ will start by MAKING the units match (sixths) — equivalent fractions again.

steps.title: Past the whole, and back from it
beats: Sums can pass a whole: $\frac{5}{6} + \frac{4}{6} = \frac{9}{6}$ — top-heavy. Convert: $1\frac{3}{6} = 1\frac{1}{2}$.

To subtract FROM a whole, dress it in the needed name first: $1 = \frac{4}{4}$, so $1 - \frac{3}{4} = \frac{1}{4}$. For $2 - \frac{5}{8}$: take the eighths from ONE of the wholes — $1\frac{8}{8} - \frac{5}{8} = 1\frac{3}{8}$.
Receipt thinking still applies: $1\frac{3}{8} + \frac{5}{8} = 2$ ✓ — additions check subtractions here exactly as with whole numbers.

steps.title: Crossing one
steps.intro: Convert top-heavy sums; rename wholes before subtracting.

steps.title: Over and back
steps.intro: Top-heavy? Convert. From a whole? Rename first.

problems.explanation: $\frac{12}{9}$ converts: $1\frac{3}{9}$, and $\frac{3}{9}$ merges to $\frac{1}{3}$.
$1 = \frac{5}{5}$: five fifths minus two is three — $\frac{3}{5}$.
Take the quarters from one whole: $2\frac{4}{4} - \frac{3}{4} = 2\frac{1}{4}$; receipt $2\frac{1}{4} + \frac{3}{4} = 3$ ✓.

steps.title: Rename, then count
steps.prompt: To compute $1 - \frac{5}{12}$, the first move is:
steps.explanation: Dress the whole in twelfths, then count: $\frac{12}{12} - \frac{5}{12} = \frac{7}{12}$.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Like denominators: add or subtract the COUNTS; the name stays.
A sum smaller than an addend means the denominators were added — the alarm bell.
Top-heavy results convert to mixed numbers; simplify what merges.
Subtracting from wholes: rename the whole first (1 = n/n) — and receipt the answer.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: Simplify every answer and receipt every subtraction — the two finishing moves that separate done from almost-done.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: The full like-denominator toolkit.

problems.prompt: A jug holds $1$ litre; $\frac{3}{8}$ has been poured out. Remaining:
You walk $\frac{4}{5}$ km to school and $\frac{4}{5}$ km back. Total:
problems.explanation: $\frac{4}{5} + \frac{4}{5} = \frac{8}{5} = 1\frac{3}{5}$ km — past one whole kilometre, as a there-and-back should be. ($\frac{8}{10}$ added the names.)
The sixths add: $\frac{1}{6} + \frac{4}{6} = \frac{5}{6}$, riding with the $2$: $2\frac{5}{6}$.

steps.title: You've finished "Adding & Subtracting Fractions" — and the topic
steps.body: Parts of a whole, many names for one amount, size against count, two names for top-heavy amounts, and same-name arithmetic: the complete first tour of fractions. Different denominators — and the equivalent-fraction bridge that tames them — are where Grade 6 picks up the story.

practice.statement: A cake is cut into $12$ equal pieces and $7$ are eaten. What fraction remains?
practice.solution: $12 - 7 = 5$ pieces of the twelfth size: $\frac{5}{12}$. Check: $\frac{7}{12} + \frac{5}{12} = 1$.
Six equal groups of $7$; take five: $35$.
Same count — finer cuts are smaller: $\frac{5}{11} < \frac{5}{9} < \frac{5}{7}$.

practice.statement: Write $\frac{47}{9}$ as a mixed number, with its receipt.

practice.solution: $\frac{14}{14} = 1$ — the pieces rebuild the whole exactly.

practice.statement: A bottle holds $2$ litres; $\frac{7}{10}$ of a litre is poured out. How much remains?
practice.solution: Take the tenths from one whole: $1\frac{10}{10} - \frac{7}{10} = 1\frac{3}{10}$ litres. Receipt: $1\frac{3}{10} + \frac{7}{10} = 2$ ✓.

testYourself.statement: Which is larger, $\frac{7}{12}$ or $\frac{4}{9}$? Use the half benchmark.
Write $5\frac{4}{7}$ as an improper fraction, and $\frac{34}{8}$ as a simplified mixed number.
Compute $\frac{8}{15} + \frac{11}{15}$, giving the answer as a mixed number.
A family eats $\frac{5}{8}$ of a bread at breakfast and $\frac{2}{8}$ at lunch. What fraction of the bread remains, and why is the answer NOT $\frac{7}{16}$ eaten?
testYourself.solution: Eaten: $\frac{5}{8} + \frac{2}{8} = \frac{7}{8}$ — the pieces stayed eighths; adding denominators would claim the bread was recut. Remaining: $1 - \frac{7}{8} = \frac{1}{8}$.
